title: Sales angles for inference platform — competitive field brief
content:
Purpose
This is a compact, battle-ready reference for sellers and solution engineers who must position Redwood Inference versus generic LLM API vendors and self-hosted inference vendors. Focus: short, repeatable lines, one-paragraph positioning by buyer archetype, common traps we expect from competitors, and concrete rebuttals + demo priorities.

Top-level thesis (one-liner)
Redwood: predictable inference economics and production reliability for teams who outgrow ad-hoc LLM endpoints — same API surface across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments so customers avoid forklift migrations when risk/cost/scale changes.

Buyer archetypes & one-paragraph positioning
- Product-driven startup (PLG + rapid shipping): You want fast time-to-value but predictable costs once growth happens. Pitch: hosted API for immediate velocity + usage visibility; show cost breakdown per route and intelligent batching recommendations so they see how to scale smoothly. Demo: quick integration + console cost breakdown.
- Platform/Infrastructure team at mid-market/enterprise: They need isolation, predictable latency, and rollout controls. Pitch: Dedicated pools with SLA, autoscaling policies, and model pinning; highlight network and KMS integrations. Demo: model rollouts + tracing + per-token latency SLA reporting.
- Highly regulated / on-prem shop: Compliance and data residency win. Pitch: Redwood Private — same control plane patterns, audit logs, HSM/KMS hooks, and an on-prem package; emphasize no surprises in APIs or rollout flows. Demo: private deployment checklist + audit log view.

Competitor buckets (how they win, our counters)
- LLM API-first vendors (ultra simple API, lots of models): Win: speed of integration and low friction. Risk: noisy unit economics, limited knobs for production tuning, opaque tail latency. Counter: emphasize predictable unit economics (cost/latency tradeoff controls), built-in batching/cache, and cost transparency by token/route.
- Cloud-managed endpoints from large cloud providers: Win: integration with cloud infra, enterprise contracts. Risk: models sometimes lag, limited inference optimizations across hardware. Counter: highlight our serving runtime optimizations and quantization/ops recommendations plus ability to deploy private when needed.
- Self-hosted runtime vendors / open-source stacks: Win: control and lower sticker price (apparent). Risk: heavy ops burden, fragmentation across experiments, inconsistent performance. Counter: show TCO comparisons including SRE/headcount and time-to-stable-performance; demo how Redwood removes brittle orchestration work.

Common objections + concise rebuttals (scripted)
- "We can just use the big cloud provider — cheaper with reserved VMs."
  - Rebuttal: Reserved VMs hide a lot of non-obvious costs (SRE time, model tuning, failed rollouts). We give measurable unit economics (tokens + latency) and automation for batching/fallbacks to avoid risk. Offer: run a 2-week pilot with workload samples to project real TCO and latency SLO attainment.
- "Open-source runtimes are flexible and avoid vendor lock-in."
  - Rebuttal: Definitely an option if you have 3–4 FTEs dedicated to inference infra. Redwood accelerates time-to-results and reduces headcount risk by providing maintenance, model variant compatibility, and cross-environment consistency. Offer: present a week-by-week migration plan with stop-gap self-hosted fallback.
- "How is Redwood different from your hosted competitors who support 100s of models?"
  - Rebuttal: Model breadth is table stakes; differentiation is predictability and observability under production load. Walk through our console telemetry: per-route latency histograms, trace links, token-level cost, and automatic fallback policies.

Trap cards (things to avoid and how to steer the buyer)
- Trap: Letting the conversation get stuck on model zoo size.
  - Steering: Reframe to workload patterns (seq length, qps, tail latency) and ask for sample requests. Then show how our runtime and routing policies map to those patterns.
- Trap: Deep technical dive into architecture with non-technical procurement stakeholders.
  - Steering: Present the outcomes first (SLA, cost per 1M tokens, rollout cadence). Technical appendix available on demand.
- Trap: Competitor claims of "always-cheaper" pricing.
  - Steering: Request a real sample workload. Pricing comparisons must use identical workload: batching, cache hits, and sequence distribution materially affect cost. Offer to run a benchmark with their 24–48 hour trace.

Demo playbook (10-minute core demo + 10-minute deep dives)
- 0–2 min: One-line value prop + customer archetype.
- 2–6 min: Live integration (send sample request), show latency, tokens, and streaming response.
- 6–10 min: Console: per-route cost breakdown, autoscale config, and a canary rollout UI. Emphasize the identical API for hosted and private modes.
- 10–20 min (optional deep dive): show model fallback policy, KV/prefix caching, and trace from request to GPU instance. For infra audiences, pull up kernel/quantization suggestions and the inferred cost impact.

Proof points & quick numbers to memorize
- Typical median latency improvement vs naive HTTP endpoints: 20–40% (varies by seq length).
- Common TCO delta vs self-hosted (including 2 FTE ops + infra): 30–60% over 12 months for production workloads.
- Pilot turnaround: 1–2 weeks for hosted sandbox; 4–8 weeks for Dedicated/on-prem proof-of-concept.
(Include numbers with a caveat: dependent on workload — always follow with an offer to run a short benchmark.)

Play examples (one-liners to hand to reps)
- For founders: "Ship now — avoid surprises later. We’ll show the exact token cost and latency you’ll see at 10x growth in one afternoon."
- For infra leads: "Predictable latency and rollback controls so your product teams can safely rely on LLMs in production."
- For compliance/legal: "Private deployments, audit trails, and KMS integrations — same developer ergonomics as our hosted API."

Open items / follow-ups (TO-DOs for GTM)
- Collect two anonymized sample workloads from current trials for benchmark collateral (Owner: Connor).
- Create a short one-page cheat sheet for AE/SDRs with the demo playbook and 3 memorized numbers (Owner: Lina).
- Build a short benchmark template (1–2 scripts) that SEs can run with customer traces (Owner: Ravi).

Notes to self
- Keep rebuttals concise — sales will read only the top 3 lines. This doc is meant for SE + AE quick prep, not a 20-page whitepaper.
- Iterate after 3 live deals and fold in real customer quotes that reference saved headcount or avoided outages.

End.
